content_units: Ontario Repair-Entry Check for This Notice
This looks   likely improper on timing   and   possibly improper on entry hours   under Ontario residential tenancy rules.
For a repair or inspection entry, tenants generally look for   written notice at least 24 hours in advance  , a   reasonable time between 8:00 AM and 8:00 PM  , and a stated reason.
Tenant Checklist for a Bathroom-Leak Entry Notice
Step   Action   What to Check   Expected Result
1   Save the notice   Keep screenshot/email/text/letter with sent time   Proof of exact notice details
2   Check 24-hour timing   Notice sent   2026-02-03 18:00  ; entry set   2026-02-04 08:30     Only   14.5 hours   notice; likely not valid for routine entry
3   Check time-of-day window   Proposed entry is   08:30 AM     Within the usual   8 AM–8 PM   window
4   Check reason given   “  Inspect bathroom leak  ”   Reason is specific enough for repair/inspection context
5   Check for emergency facts   Active flooding, burst pipe, unit damage risk, danger?   If true emergency, landlord may enter without 24-hour notice
6   Keep repair history   Photos, leak reports, prior requests, maintenance messages   Shows whether issue is ongoing or urgent
7   Reply in writing   Be polite; ask to reschedule with proper notice unless emergency   Clear record of cooperation
8   Document outcome   If they enter or attempt entry, note time, who came, what happened   Helpful if dispute escalates
Practical Read on Your Specific Scenario
-   Notice timing:   Sent at   6:00 PM on Feb 3   for   8:30 AM on Feb 4   is   not 24 hours  . For a normal repair/inspection entry, that is   likely defective notice  .
-   Entry hour:     8:30 AM   is generally   within permitted daytime hours  .
-   Reason:   “  Inspect bathroom leak  ” is usually a sufficiently stated purpose.

-   Key exception:   If the leak is a   true emergency  —for example active water damage, flooding, risk to other units, or urgent building damage—the landlord may have stronger grounds to enter sooner.
Polite Response You Can Send
You asked for a practical, non-confrontational reply. You can send:

“Hello [Landlord/Property Manager], thank you for letting me know about the bathroom leak inspection. I want to cooperate and provide access. However, the notice sent on February 3 at 6:00 PM for entry on February 4 at 8:30 AM appears to provide less than 24 hours’ notice. If this is not an emergency, please send a new notice with at least 24 hours and I will make reasonable efforts to accommodate entry. If you believe this is an emergency, please let me know the urgent risk involved. Thank you.”
Shorter version:

“Thanks for the notice. I’m happy to cooperate with leak inspection, but this appears to be less than 24 hours’ notice. If it’s not an emergency, please resend with proper notice and I’ll arrange access.”
Records to Keep if You Want to Protect Yourself
- Copy of the notice with   date, time, method of delivery
- Screenshot of your   reply
- Photos/video of the   bathroom leak condition
- Any earlier maintenance requests about the leak
- Log of:
- when the landlord contacted you
- when anyone arrived
- names of workers or staff
- whether entry happened
- what work was done
- If you speak by phone or in person, send a short follow-up message:
“Confirming our call today at 7:10 PM…”
